note: Second-pass CRE Set 3 calculations on high-weight models. Not copied from Set 2. Each display equation is on its own line.

questions.stem:
Life follows a two-parameter Weibull model. The shape is \(\beta\), the characteristic life is \(\eta\), and the age is \(t\). Use \(e^{-0.25}=0.7788\) and \(e^{-0.50}=0.6065\).
\[
R(t)=\exp[-(t/\eta)^{\beta}]
\]
What is the reliability at 500 hours?
questions.why: Square the time ratio before taking the exponential. Do not report the unreliability. \[ (t/\eta)^{\beta}=(500/1000)^{2}=0.25 \] \[ R(500)=\exp(-0.25)=0.7788 \] 0.6065 drops the square. 0.2500 stops at the exponent. 0.2212 is \(1-R(500)\). D. 0.7788

chart.title: Weibull life model
chart.altText: Shape beta is 2. Characteristic life eta is 1,000 hours. The reliability is asked at 500 hours.

questions.stem:
The same Weibull model has shape \(\beta\) and characteristic life \(\eta\). The B10 life is the age at which reliability is still 0.90. Use \(-\ln 0.90=0.10536\).
\[
t_{10}=\eta(-\ln 0.90)^{1/\beta}
\]
What is the B10 life, to one decimal place?
questions.why: Take the square root of 0.10536, then scale by the characteristic life. \[ t_{10}=1000(0.10536)^{0.5} \] \[ t_{10}=1000(0.3246)=324.6 \] 105.4 hours skips the root. 500 hours is half of eta. 1,000 hours is eta itself, which is about the B63 life for this model, not the B10 life. B. 324.6 hours

traps.A: Multiplies eta by 0.10536 and does not take the root.
traps.C: Uses half of the characteristic life.

chart.title: Weibull B10 inputs
chart.altText: Shape beta is 2. Characteristic life eta is 1,000 hours. B10 is the age where reliability is 0.90. The natural log constant is given in the question.

questions.stem:
A lognormal life has parameters \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) on the natural-log scale. Use \(e^{4}=54.598\) and \(e^{0.5}=1.6487\).
\[
t_{mean}=\exp(\mu+\sigma^{2}/2)
\]
What is the mean life, to two decimal places?
questions.why: The mean is larger than the median. Add \(\sigma^{2}/2\), not \(\sigma\). \[ \sigma^{2}/2=0.50 \] \[ t_{mean}=e^{4}\,e^{0.5}=54.598(1.6487)=90.02 \] 54.60 hours is the median, \(e^{\mu}\). 27.30 hours multiplies the median by \(\sigma^{2}/2\) instead of by \(e^{\sigma^{2}/2}\). 148.41 hours uses \(e^{\mu+\sigma}\). C. 90.02 hours

traps.D: Adds sigma instead of sigma squared over 2.

chart.title: Lognormal parameters
chart.altText: mu is 4 and sigma is 1, both on the natural-log scale of life in hours.

questions.stem:
Three independent exponential elements operate in series. The system fails when any one fails. Failure rates are \(\lambda_1\), \(\lambda_2\), and \(\lambda_3\).
\[
\lambda_s=\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3
\]
\[
MTTF=\frac{1}{\lambda_s}
\]
What is the system MTTF?
questions.why: Add the failure rates. Do not add or average the individual mean lives. \[ \lambda_s=0.001+0.001+0.002=0.004 \] \[ MTTF=\frac{1}{0.004}=250 \] 500 hours is the shortest element life. 833 hours averages the three mean lives. 2,500 hours adds them. A. 250 hours

traps.B: Uses only the largest failure rate.
traps.C: Averages the three element mean lives.
traps.D: Adds the three element mean lives.

chart.title: Series exponential elements
chart.altText: Three independent elements are in series. Their failure rates are 0.001, 0.001, and 0.002 failures per hour.

questions.stem:
One unit operates and an identical unit is in cold standby. The switch is perfect, and the standby unit does not fail while waiting. Use \(e^{-1}=0.3679\). At the stated age, \(\lambda t=1\).
\[
R(t)=e^{-\lambda t}(1+\lambda t)
\]
What is the mission reliability?
questions.why: A perfect cold standby adds the \(\lambda t\) term. It is not an active parallel pair. \[ R(t)=0.3679(1+1)=0.7358 \] 0.3679 is one unit with no standby credit. 0.6004 is an active parallel pair. 0.1353 is the two units in series. D. 0.7358

traps.A: Multiplies the two unit reliabilities as if both must survive.
traps.C: Uses an active parallel pair instead of cold standby.

chart.title: Cold-standby mission
chart.altText: The operating failure rate is 0.01 per hour. Mission time is 100 hours, so lambda t is 1. The spare is in cold standby and the switch is perfect.

questions.stem:
Life follows an inverse power model in voltage. \(S_s\) is the stress voltage, \(S_u\) is the use voltage, and \(n\) is the given exponent.
\[
AF=(S_s/S_u)^{n}
\]
What is the acceleration factor?
questions.why: The voltage ratio is raised to the exponent. It is not multiplied by the exponent. \[ S_s/S_u=40/20=2 \] \[ AF=2^{3}=8 \] 2 is the voltage ratio. 6 multiplies that ratio by 3. 9 squares 3. C. 8

traps.B: Multiplies the ratio by the exponent.
traps.D: Squares the exponent instead of raising the ratio.

chart.title: Inverse-power voltage test
chart.altText: Use voltage is 20 V. Stress voltage is 40 V. The inverse-power exponent n is 3.

questions.stem:
A Crow-AMSAA growth model has scale \(\lambda\) and growth parameter \(\beta\). At total test time \(T\), the value \(T^{\beta-1}\) is given. The instantaneous failure intensity is
\[
\lambda_i(T)=\lambda\beta T^{\beta-1}
\]
What is \(\lambda_i(T)\)?
questions.why: Multiply the scale, the growth parameter, and the given power of time. The cumulative intensity omits \(\beta\). \[ \lambda_i(100)=0.5(0.5)(0.10)=0.025 \] 0.050 is \(\lambda T^{\beta-1}\), the cumulative intensity. 0.250 is \(\lambda\beta\). 0.500 is the scale alone. A. 0.025

traps.B: Drops beta and reports the cumulative intensity.

chart.title: Crow-AMSAA growth model
chart.altText: Lambda is 0.5, beta is 0.5, and total test time is 100 hours. T to the power beta minus 1 equals 0.10.

questions.stem:
Failures are exponential with mean life 200 hours. A unit already has 500 hours of operation. Use \(e^{-0.5}=0.6065\) and \(e^{-2.5}=0.0821\).
\[
R(t+t_0\mid t)=R(t_0)
\]
What is the probability that it survives the next 100 hours?
questions.why: The exponential distribution is memoryless. Age does not change the reliability over the next interval. \[ R(100)=e^{-100/200}=0.6065 \] 0.0821 is the reliability of a new unit through 500 hours, not through the next 100. 0.5000 divides 100 by 200 and treats the ratio as a probability. 0.1353 is \(e^{-2}\). C. 0.6065

traps.A: Uses the survival probability from time zero to the current age.
traps.B: Treats time divided by the mean as the reliability.
traps.D: Uses a 200-hour interval instead of 100 hours.

chart.title: Exponential unit age
chart.altText: Mean life theta is 200 hours. The unit has already operated 500 hours. The next interval asked is 100 hours.

questions.stem: A supplier asks to be added to the approved-parts list. The evidence is below. Purchasing notes that the parts are already on the dock. Which decision is supported?
options: Approve the supplier. A dock receipt is a completed reliability assessment.
Approve the supplier. Two failures are close enough to a zero-failure rule.
Do not approve the supplier. The demonstration failed and no corrective action is shown.
Approve the supplier for one lot. An open demonstration can be closed after the parts are used.
questions.why: Supplier acceptance uses the stated reliability evidence. The accept rule was zero failures, the lot had two, and no corrective action is shown. A dock receipt does not close that gap, and using the parts does not convert a failed demonstration into a pass. C. Do not approve the supplier. The demonstration failed and no corrective action is shown.

traps.A: Replaces the reliability evidence with a receiving stamp.
traps.B: Relaxes a zero-failure rule after the failures are known.
traps.D: Defers the decision until after the unapproved parts are used.

chart.title: Supplier reliability evidence
chart.altText: The demonstration accept rule was zero failures. The result was two failures. No corrective action was shown. Purchasing reports that the parts are on the dock.

questions.stem:
A series system has a reliability requirement \(R_s\). The requirement is apportioned equally to \(n\) independent elements by
\[
R_i=R_s^{1/n}
\]
What is the required element reliability, to four decimal places?
questions.why: Equal reliability apportionment takes the n-th root. It does not divide the reliability by n, and it is not the equal split of unreliability. \[ R_i=0.960^{1/3}=0.9865 \] 0.3200 divides 0.960 by 3. 0.9600 copies the system requirement onto one element. 0.9867 splits the 0.040 unreliability into three equal parts. C. 0.9865

traps.A: Divides the system reliability by the number of elements.
traps.B: Assigns the system goal to every element.
traps.D: Uses an equal-unreliability split instead of the stated root.

chart.title: Equal reliability apportionment
chart.altText: The series system requirement is 0.960. It is apportioned equally to 3 independent elements by the cube root.
